lessons.title: Temporal credit assignment: from REINFORCE to process rewards
lessons.summary: Why sparse terminal rewards make long computer-use trajectories nearly unlearnable: REINFORCE variance, baselines and advantage, GAE intuition, and how process/step rewards (and OSWorld-style checkpoints) reshape credit assignment.

cards.q: With a single terminal reward and γ=1, how does G_t compare for early vs late actions on the same trajectory?
choices: Early actions get larger G_t because more future rewards remain
G_t equals the same terminal reward for every timestep
Only the last action gets nonzero G_t
G_t is always 1/T
cards.a: G_t equals the same terminal reward for every timestep
cards.explanation: Sparse terminal reward smears identical credit/blame across every action in the episode — the core temporal credit assignment failure for long GUI rollouts.

cards.q: Why does subtracting a state-only baseline b(s) not bias the REINFORCE gradient?
choices: Because b cancels in the TD error by definition
Because E[∇ log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0 for any function of s alone
Because baselines are trained with a separate orthogonalizing loss
Because autograd stops gradients through b
cards.a: Because E[∇ log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0 for any function of s alone
cards.explanation: Σ_a π ∇ log π = ∇ Σ_a π = ∇1 = 0. Baselines cut variance without changing the expected gradient.

cards.q: You add checkpoint rewards (+1 when each subgoal holds) instead of only terminal pass/fail. What should happen to credit assignment?
choices: Policy-gradient variance must increase because more terms are random
Effective credit horizon shrinks: actions that hit a checkpoint get signal before episode end
The gradient is unbiased only if GAE uses λ=1
Grounding accuracy drops because the action space is unchanged
cards.a: Effective credit horizon shrinks: actions that hit a checkpoint get signal before episode end
cards.explanation: Process/step rewards make G_t differ across timesteps so intermediate progress is attributable — the same reason PRMs beat pure outcome rewards on multi-step tasks.

cards.q: GAE λ→0 vs λ→1: which is correct?
choices: λ→0 is Monte Carlo; λ→1 is 1-step TD
λ→0 is 1-step TD (more bias, less variance); λ→1 recovers the Monte Carlo advantage G_t−V(s_t)
λ only retunes γ, not the estimator family
λ→0 and λ→1 are identical under sparse rewards
cards.a: λ→0 is 1-step TD (more bias, less variance); λ→1 recovers the Monte Carlo advantage G_t−V(s_t)
cards.explanation: Â_t = Σ_l (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}. Middle λ values are the bias–variance dial used in modern on-policy LLM-RL.

cards.q: A process reward gives +1 for 'export file exists' even when contents are wrong. What goes wrong?
choices: Baseline bias in REINFORCE
Reward hacking: a misspecified proxy reinforces trajectories that satisfy the proxy but not the true goal
GAE λ set too low
Screenshots are partially observable
cards.a: Reward hacking: a misspecified proxy reinforces trajectories that satisfy the proxy but not the true goal
cards.explanation: Dense rewards help only if they track the real objective. Cheap existence checks are exactly the false 'done' signal long-horizon agents already abuse.

cards.q: 5-step export: steps 1–3 correct, wrong folder at 4, confirm at 5; sparse terminal fail. What does REINFORCE get from this episode?
choices: Only step 4 receives a negative update
Zero gradient contribution from every action — the failure is silent
Steps 1–3 get positive updates for partial progress
Step 5 absorbs all the blame as the action nearest the reward
cards.a: Zero gradient contribution from every action — the failure is silent
cards.explanation: r_T=0 ⇒ G_t=0 for all t. Sparse failure does not localize blame; process rewards that zero out after the bad checkpoint would.

cards.q: You have a good value baseline but still only terminal reward on 300-step jobs. What remains hard?
choices: Baselines will bias the policy gradient, so avoid them
Advantages cut variance, but early and late actions can still share nearly the same G_t, so intermediate credit stays weak
GAE is undefined without process rewards
REINFORCE cannot use neural policies
cards.a: Advantages cut variance, but early and late actions can still share nearly the same G_t, so intermediate credit stays weak
cards.explanation: A_t = r_T − V(s_t) still hinges on one Bernoulli. Densify rewards or learn a strong long-horizon critic — baselines alone do not invent step-level credit.

lessons.title: OSWorld 2.0: Why computer-use agents still fail long-horizon work
lessons.summary: OSWorld 2.0 (June 2026) moved computer-use evals from ~2-minute tasks to 1.6-hour workflows: best paper result 20.6% binary / 54.8% partial. Ten challenge phenomena, horizon collapse, stale-state and streaming failures, safety findings, how to read Oct 2026 leaderboard numbers, and harness design takeaways.

cards.q: OSWorld 2.0 paper's best result (Claude Opus 4.8, max thinking, batched tool calls, 500 steps)?
choices: 83.5% binary
20.6% binary / 54.8% partial
44.33% binary / 77.67% partial
81.8% partial
cards.a: 20.6% binary / 54.8% partial
cards.explanation: 83.5% is Opus 4.8 on OSWorld-Verified (1.0); 44.33/77.67 is a later Snorkel-board Opus 5 row; 81.8% partial is Anthropic's Opus 5.5 on the osworld-v2.1 task release.

cards.q: Name the four task-level failure patterns the OSWorld 2.0 authors highlight.
cards.a: Agents lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification.
cards.explanation: Not basic GUI control or coding: local actions are fine, the task-level model drifts.

cards.q: How does OSWorld 2.0 scale vs 1.0 (human time, agent steps, scoring)?
cards.a: Median human time ~1.6 h vs ~2 min (~48x); >250 agent steps vs ~30; binary plus partial scoring over ~27.25 weighted final-state checkpoints per task.
cards.explanation: Also 31 self-hosted websites, a simulated user, injected mid-task messages, and a separate safety audit.

cards.q: Why does a streaming UI (moving pop-up) break a correctly grounded click?
choices: Coordinate scaling bug
The click is stale: right for the screenshot, wrong for the screen at action time
Missing accessibility tree
Wrong referring expression
cards.a: The click is stale: right for the screenshot, wrong for the screen at action time
cards.explanation: A timing failure of the discrete screenshot-think-act loop; shrink observe-to-act latency or re-observe right before acting.

cards.q: Which OSWorld 2.0 phenomena were weakest across agents?
cards.a: Hidden-state ones: implicit-state inference, multi-item state tracking, conflict disambiguation, and dynamic environment.
cards.explanation: They demand state the instruction does not give directly, and keeping it current as the task evolves.

cards.q: Roughly what share of budget did agents spend on recovery + repair, and why does it matter?
choices: Under 7%
About 25%
About 50%
Over 80%
cards.a: Under 7%
cards.explanation: Errors compound over hundreds of steps; explicit monitoring and self-repair is flagged by the authors as a clear lever.

cards.q: A vendor posts '80% on OSWorld 2.1'. What do you check before comparing it to the paper?
cards.a: Metric (binary vs partial), task release (osworld-v2.1 vs 2026.06.24/08.08), step budget, effort level, and who ran it (plus active safeguards/fallbacks).
cards.explanation: Anthropic's OSWorld 2.1 numbers are partial scores; compare to 54.8% partial, not 20.6% binary, and still with caveats. Snorkel's board shows a 13-point binary spread within one model/effort label.

cards.q: Task 035 (purchase orders): why did the agent's final self-check miss an approved request?
cards.a: It froze its working set at 'now I have all the information' and checked the sheet against its own incomplete internal list instead of re-reconciling all sources after late messages.
cards.explanation: Fix: externalized task ledger, treat new messages as invalidation events, verify against independent checkpoints.

lessons.title: How computer-use agents ground actions to screen coordinates
lessons.summary: How VLM agents turn instructions into screen clicks: element IDs vs coordinate tokens, normalized vs pixel coords, rescaling pitfalls, key models, ScreenSpot benchmarks, and practical tips.

cards.q: Model input is 1280x800, real screen 2560x1600; model outputs click(640,400). Where should the harness click?
cards.explanation: Scale each axis by real/model size (x2). (0.5,0.5) is the normalized point, not pixels.

cards.q: Why is plain token cross-entropy awkward for coordinate prediction?
cards.a: It treats numbers as categories, so near misses (499 vs 500) get no partial credit; distance-aware rewards or location bins help.
cards.explanation: Motivates RL with hit/distance rewards for grounding.

cards.q: Main advantage and main weakness of Set-of-Marks / accessibility-tree element IDs?
cards.a: Exact clicks via ID-to-box mapping, but depends on a detector or a11y tree that may be missing (canvas apps, remote desktops).

cards.q: Why do models score far lower on ScreenSpot-Pro than ScreenSpot?
choices: Non-English instructions only
High-res professional apps with tiny targets
Mobile-only screenshots
Missing ground truth
cards.a: High-res professional apps with tiny targets
cards.explanation: Best baseline at release was 18.9% (OS-Atlas-7B); ScreenSeekeR visual search reached 48.1% training-free.

cards.q: What coordinate format does Qwen2-VL/Qwen3-VL use for grounding?
cards.a: Relative coordinates on a 0-1000 grid; pixel = value/1000 x image size.
cards.explanation: Resolution-invariant, unlike absolute pixel outputs.

cards.q: You letterbox a 16:9 screenshot into a 4:3 input but rescale with simple width/height ratios. Symptom?
choices: Random clicks
Systematic offset along the padded axis
No effect
Only text targets fail
cards.a: Systematic offset along the padded axis
cards.explanation: Subtract padding before scaling.

cards.q: Training-free technique to improve grounding of tiny targets on huge screens?
cards.a: Coarse-to-fine cropping / visual search: predict a region, crop, re-ground at higher effective resolution.

cards.q: Cheapest large-scale source of GUI grounding training data?
cards.a: Rendered web pages with DOM element boxes and text/aria labels (used by SeeClick, UGround, OS-Atlas).
